newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders reaffirm mid-1997 target for reforms.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders reaffirm mid-1997 target for reforms.

text.p: European Union leaders reaffirmed on Saturday that negotiations for a treaty to reform the bloc ahead of taking in new members should end by the middle of next year.
During a working lunch at the start of a special one-day summit in Dublin, several also urged the bloc to aim for ambitious changes and not to lower their sights.
"June 1997 is a desirable and realistic target but not at the cost of substance," Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told reporters.

Leaders were at pains to deny they were scaling down their ambitions, after speculation prompted by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's comments that more reforms would be needed to EU institutions even after the current treaty talks, known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC).
"We have to get the EU ready for enlargement. This won't be possible without getting results at the IGC," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told reporters.
Asked whether France and Germany had reduced their ambitions, Kinkel said: "No, that's not true. France and Germany together remain the motor."
Diplomats quoted Kohl as saying that he remained ambitious but that the Treaty of Rome, which founded the EU's forerunner, the European Economic Community, had itself been modified many times.
"Perhaps in a few years others may be more intelligent than us and will want to make more changes," he was quoted as saying.
Germany's IGC negotiator, State Secretary Werner Hoyer, said countries in central and eastern Europe needed to know where they stood by the year 2000.
"If enlargement doesn't come, people in eastern Europe will feel such a frustration that this could turn into a security risk for us at some point in time," he said.
Diplomats said no one suggested during the lunch discussion that the goal of agreeing a treaty at the summit scheduled for Amsterdam next June should be changed.

The prospect of British general elections next May has prompted speculation that a hostile Conservative government would block much progress before then while any new Labour government would need more than a month to conclude a treaty.
